section_summary: This section documents the April 10, 1946 Japanese general election, including pre-election maneuvering, Soviet and British press criticism, State and War Department discussion of occupation policy, preliminary results, and competing plans for a post-election coalition cabinet. It contains a comprehensive roster of major-party officials, a Political Adviser report analyzing turnout, women voters, registration problems, party strength, constitutional policy, and the possible continuation of Prime Minister Shidehara. The final pages comprise the Japanese-language Asahi and Mainichi election issues forwarded for their biographical directories of successful candidates, together with editorials, election tables, political commentary, and other contemporary news.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of report on pre-election party maneuvering and coalition prospects
subfiles.about: Concludes an analysis of Hatoyama's coalition proposal and efforts to retain Shidehara as prime minister after the election.
subfiles.summary: Hatoyama's approach to Social Democratic leaders is interpreted as an effort to moderate his reactionary reputation and prepare a Liberal-led coalition. Communist leader Nosaka attacks the proposal, while rumors circulate of a broader government party supporting Shidehara or Mitsuchi. Sebald concludes that post-election realignment is likely, but doubts that the current party leaders possess the prestige and leadership needed for a stable cabinet.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1135: Izvestiya on pre-election conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Moscow, via War Department
subfiles.about: Summarizes Soviet criticism of the timing and political conditions of Japan's April 1946 election.
subfiles.summary: Izvestiya's Tokyo correspondent portrays Japanese voters, especially women, as politically unprepared and vulnerable to conservative or clerical influence. The article alleges that occupation authorities favor Shidehara's reactionary government, condemns the Social Democrats for rejecting a Communist united front, and claims that rightist parties enjoy superior funding and paper supplies. A TASS item also outlines the Democratic People's League's call for a popular-front government, a democratic constitution, economic planning, and the destruction of militarist and monopolistic power.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Tokyo's election-policy telegram
subfiles.about: Records a State–War Department discussion of Bishop's recommendation that occupation policy support non-Communist Japanese political groups.
subfiles.summary: Braisted reports G-2 concern that Bishop has oversimplified Japanese politics into Communist and non-Communist camps and that blanket support for non-Communists could conflict with the January 4 purge directive. Borton and Emmerson agree that ultranationalists may be found among non-Communists and urge evaluation of individuals rather than labels. The participants also doubt that the Far Eastern Commission would invalidate the election, despite earlier concern that it was being held too soon.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1149: Pravda on the Emperor, constitution, and election
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Moscow, via War Department
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Pravda editorial attacking the imperial institution, the Shidehara government, and the occupation-sponsored constitution.
subfiles.summary: Pravda correspondent Boris Gorbatov presents the fate of the Emperor as the central issue of Japanese politics and endorses the Communist demand to abolish the imperial system and try Hirohito with Tojo. The article argues that the Emperor's democratized public image strengthens reactionaries and that fascist officials, generals, police, and capitalists remain entrenched. It also condemns the draft constitution for legalizing a constitutional monarchy and cites British criticism of U.S. tolerance for the old ruling clique.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 370: List of officers of major Japanese political parties
subfiles.from: Officer in Charge, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a party-supplied roster of officers and committee members of Japan's five principal political parties as of April 5, 1946.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure lists the leadership, committees, secretariats, and departmental chiefs of the Progressive, Liberal, Cooperative, Socialist, and Communist parties. It provides unusually detailed organizational information, including women's, election, labor, agricultural, propaganda, publication, cultural, research, and finance posts. Hatoyama, Katayama, Tokuda, Nosaka, and numerous other national political figures appear in the roster.

subfiles.title: Telegram 4141: British press reaction to the Japanese election
subfiles.from: George H. Gallman, U.S. Embassy London
subfiles.to: Department of State and Allied Commander, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews British editorials and feature articles on Japan's election, constitution, occupation, reparations, and industrial power.
subfiles.summary: The Yorkshire Post, Observer, Times, and Manchester Guardian question whether formally free elections can produce democracy amid apathy, uncertainty, unchanged administration, and surviving militarist influence. They urge early clarification of peace terms and reparations and criticize MacArthur for accepting Japan's conversion too readily. Reports by J. Deane Potter and Owen Lattimore emphasize continuing rightist networks and warn that industrial capacity could again threaten Asian peace unless surplus plant is transferred to neighboring countries.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1218: Soviet press response after the election
subfiles.from: Walter Bedell Smith, U.S. Embassy Moscow
subfiles.about: Reports the Soviet press's initial post-election silence and its focus on defective voter-registration lists.
subfiles.summary: Moscow newspapers had not yet published factual results or even announced that the April 10 election occurred. Their likely line is indicated by reports that nearly one million eligible voters were omitted from registration lists and that the Japanese Communist Party demanded a new election with better lists and stricter candidate verification.

subfiles.title: DC/R routing slip
subfiles.about: Routes the preceding telegram for action and distribution.
subfiles.summary: A brief administrative routing sheet directs the associated record to the relevant action office and notes the number of copies. It contains no substantive political analysis.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 379: Political Parties in Japan—Developments During the Week Ending April 13, 1946
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a detailed report on the April 10 election results, voter participation, party strength, and post-election cabinet negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates turnout at about 72 percent, notes the independent participation of women and election of 38 women, and gives preliminary party totals showing a Liberal plurality with strong Progressive and Social Democratic contingents. It judges the electorate broadly conservative but identifies a significant desire for change, dismisses most registration defects as products of wartime disruption rather than official negligence, and anticipates gradual development of democratic legislative practice. Post-election analysis considers a Hatoyama or Shidehara coalition, a new government party organized by Narahashi, Mitsuchi, and Ishiguro, or a disciplined Socialist opposition. Appendices compare the five parties' policies on the Emperor, food, inflation, industrial reconstruction, unemployment, and land; reproduce Shidehara's election appeal quoting the Emperor; and tabulate successful candidates by prefecture.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 381: Biographical data on successful Diet candidates
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of the April 14 Asahi and Mainichi containing names and biographical information for successful Diet candidates.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser recommends the original Japanese newspaper material to the Division of Japanese Affairs and the Office of Research and Information. Staff limitations prevented translation, so three copies of each newspaper were transmitted under separate cover.

subfiles.title: Asahi, April 14, 1946: election results and candidate biographies
subfiles.about: Provides Japanese-language election analysis, returns, candidate biographies, and related domestic and international news.
subfiles.summary: The issue reports the Liberal plurality, debates whether the Shidehara cabinet should remain or resign, discusses Socialist strategy and a possible three-party coalition, and comments on the strength of conservative and democratic forces. Extensive tables and biographical sketches identify successful candidates by party and prefecture, with particular attention to the unprecedented number of women elected. Other articles cover the Tokyo food crisis, voter sentiment, election-law violations, returning civilians from Java and Sumatra, labor disputes, war-crimes proceedings, and international diplomacy in Europe and the Middle East.

subfiles.title: The Mainichi, April 14, 1946: directory of elected representatives and post-election commentary
subfiles.about: Presents a Japanese-language directory of elected representatives, detailed returns, and commentary on the formation and responsibilities of the new Diet.
subfiles.summary: The newspaper prints portraits or biographical entries for successful candidates from Tokyo and numerous prefectures, alongside updated vote totals and notices of required re-elections in Tokyo and Fukui. Political reporting follows negotiations among the Liberal, Progressive, and Socialist parties, the expected resignation of the Shidehara cabinet, and debate over whether Socialists should join a coalition or organize an opposition and broader democratic front. Editorial commentators urge scrutiny and possible recall of unsuitable legislators while emphasizing constitutional revision, economic reconstruction, labor rights, food policy, and resistance to surviving reactionary influence.
